essential: Tommy wakes in pain in the Soho house and recognises the German's voice. He feigns unconsciousness briefly, then is revived with a drink.
Establish who is present: the German, Conrad named as the doorkeeper who struck him, Boris, and the others. Number One is absent.
Tommy's nonchalant banter with Conrad and the German (the thick skull, the faithful watchdog) masks frantic calculation. Keep both layers: outward flippancy and inner fear.
Keep the logical chain of the bluff: they did not kill him at once because they do not know what he knows or where he learned it.
Boris screams 'Kill him!'. Tommy counters with the password point, which prompts the working man's 'Comrades, we have been betrayed!'.
The German threatens Boris's 'pretty ways'. The shabby clerk-like man says 'He's bluffing you, Boris', and Tommy fears he has been seen through.

Tommy states the bargain: his life and liberty against the Danvers papers. He has neither the papers nor their location, only a 'theory'. He adds the pressure of 'The 29th' being less than a fortnight away.
Keep the deliberation interval: Tommy waits in the next room, flippant with Conrad, while his heart beats violently. Keep the black-cap joke.
State the terms: Tommy stays prisoner and a gang member carries out his instructions. Tommy grumbles but accepts.
Tommy demands to see Jane Finn. The German's puzzling replies make Tommy feel his hold slipping. He recovers with 'Danvers was a damned clever fellow----', which reassures the German.
Only Mr. Brown can decide about the girl. 'Shall I see him?' 'Perhaps.'
Tommy is locked in a windowless upstairs room with the four Faust pictures. Mephistopheles suggests Mr. Brown, the room is a living tomb, and the chapter ends on Tommy's dreary hopes.

Paragraph 132 (headache, hunger) can be cut, but hunger must be mentioned somewhere because the next chapter opens on it.

voice_profile: Brisk, ironic third-person narration that stays close to Tommy, and later to Tommy and Julius, in the 'Young Adventurers' manner. The comedy comes from undercutting: Tommy's flippant, schoolboy bravado ('old bean', mock-heroic asides, 'Retire, varlet') is set against honest admissions of fear ('glad they could not hear the persistent beating of his heart'). Narrative generalisation about types ('one of those young Englishmen...') and cinema or dime-novel self-consciousness recur. Dialogue does most of the work. National idiom marks each speaker: Julius's Americanisms ('Put me wise', 'Sure thing', 'gets my goat'), the German's clipped menace, Conrad's and Number 14's cockney, Annette's broken English and French. Sir James speaks in dry, evasive legal phrasing ('Coincidences are curious things'). Chapters end on hooks: a reversal, a telegram, a twist. Double-hyphen dashes, '----' for broken-off speech and underscore emphasis are characteristic and must be retained.

essential: Tommy is hungry and suspects Conrad's spite. He plans to ambush Conrad with a picture, waits, and falls asleep.
Annette brings breakfast. Tommy asks if she is Jane Finn. She says her name is Annette, speaks French and broken English, does the 'service', has heard of Jane Finn but denies she is in the house.
Tommy's comic insolence to Conrad at lunch (the Pear's soap or Watson joke) and Conrad's menacing 'little enough time you'll have to talk in'. One exchange is enough.

Tommy appeals to Annette in the evening. She refuses because the gang are 'my own people' and she is afraid. She mentions three men on the floor below. The name Jane Finn is familiar to her. She reacts with terror, then relief, at the picture; Tommy rehangs it.
Three days of inaction. Annette grows mute and suspicious. The gang are waiting for orders from Mr. Brown.
Conrad and Number 14 bind Tommy and say the bluff is exposed. A 'carriage' is ordered for the morning to avoid police in the house. Tommy wrongly guesses that Tuppence went to the police.
Annette turns out the light, mocks him, and slips him an open penknife. Tommy infers a peep-hole and that he has been watched, and wonders whether her denials were for the listeners.
Tommy cuts his bonds, injuring his wrist, waits in the dark with the picture, knocks Number 14 down with it, and locks Conrad in.
Annette's ruse: the attic, string tied to the jug, the key 'found', the men released, the crash drawing them upstairs. Keep the mechanics clear enough to follow.
Annette vanishes back upstairs, cries that he has escaped and then the triple 'Marguerite'. Tommy floors Conrad and the van driver; a bullet grazes his ear and shots follow him.
Escape across Soho, the red herring sleeper, Turkish bath, then breakfast. The newspaper portrait identifies Number 1 as Kramenin.

At Whitehall, Carter is annoyed, then urgent. Westway and the Irish Unionist M.P. are identified, and Carter stresses the stakes of the treaty. The raided house is empty and Annette gone. Carter thinks she belongs to the gang. Tuppence did not go to the police, so how did they 'twig' him? The Ritz is raised as a possibility. Tommy wrongly reads 'Marguerite' as Rita and finds Tuppence has just gone out.
optional: The 'pray God it's the latter' wake-up joke (paras 7–8) can go.
The Lord's-prayer grace over breakfast (para 20) can be cut.
Number 14's 'Talking as though you were still at the blooming _Ritz_' (para 79) can go only if Carter's 'mention of the _Ritz_' line is also cut. Remove them together or keep them together.
Shorten the policeman and 'What a guy he must look' moment (para 145).
Compress the Turkish bath and A.B.C. breakfast (paras 146–147) to a sentence, but keep the newspaper portrait.
Carter's lunch invitation and the 'I take a lot of killing' banter (paras 176–181) can be cut to one line.
risks: The attic ruse involves several mechanical steps; over-compression could make the escape confusing.

essential: Reunion at the Ritz restaurant: Julius thought Tommy was dead, as did Tuppence. The two exchange stories in summary, covering Bournemouth, the car, Sir James, Mrs. Vandemeyer's death and Jane's loss of memory.
Tommy realises that Jane's memory loss explains the gang's queer looks, and Julius praises the bluff ('I was in such a funk').
Mrs. Vandemeyer's death: chloral. Everyone suspects Mr. Brown, but Tommy says 'Mr. Brown hasn't got wings', and Julius jokes about thought transference.
The page-boy 'Henry' reports a telegram, Tuppence's request for an A.B.C. and Bradshaw, and her taxi to Charing Cross.
Julius at first pockets Tuppence's note, then admits he proposed and was refused. Tommy's swing from dazed and resentful to elated must survive. The note is handed over and read, signature included.
Henry says the telegram was crumpled and thrown in the grate with a 'Whoop!'. They find it in her room; Tommy did not send it, and Julius says 'They've got her.'
Tommy reads the train timetable, decides the boy was mistaken, and works out the hostage logic that keeps Tuppence safe until the 29th. Keep 'I've great faith in Tuppence'.

At Ebury the porter remembers no enquiry. The Moat House is desolate, and a villager and Mrs. Sweeny say it has been empty for years with the key unrequested. There is undisturbed dust, then Tuppence's brooch in the leaves.
A week of fruitless searching by car. Today is the 23rd and the 29th looms. Julius decides to go to Scotland Yard while Tommy stays.
Julius wires Tommy to Manchester and shows him Peel Edgerton's telegram. Julius: 'I thought that lawyer chap had quit!'

essential: Julius explains the arrangements. Tommy doubts that 'close as an oyster' is the real reason for Sir James's silence.
Sir James meets Tommy and mentions hearing of him from Tuppence. Tommy feels his magnetism and compares him to Carter. Sir James 'took in everything, but gave out only what he chose'.
Julius demands to know how the girl was found. Sir James evades.

Sir James's account: a street accident, the infirmary, the girl giving her name as Jane Finn, her removal to a doctor friend's house. Her memory has returned. Tommy's 'like a fairy tale' meets 'Coincidences are curious things'.
Tommy concludes that Sir James never abandoned the case and attributes the secrecy to legal habit.
The clash over visiting that night: Sir James's pistol-crack 'quite useless', and Julius backing down ('you're the boss').

Tommy's abbreviated adventures. Sir James praises him and suggests Annette 'took a fancy' to him. Tommy concedes she seems one of the gang because she went back. Sir James comments on 'Marguerite' versus Rita, notes the gang's sudden change of attitude, and wishes he had searched the house.

Tuppence's disappearance comes out. Sir James's keen questions; the kidnapping is a counter-move and Tommy had worked that out. Tommy was unknown when first held. Julius times the leak to Sunday afternoon and dismisses Mr. Brown as a bogy in favour of Kramenin. Sir James insists Mr. Brown exists and asks where the wire was handed in. He wants to see it, rebukes the wasted week, and says Jane's recovery must be kept dark.
At the doctor's house, Dr. Roylance says she asked about the Lusitania survivors. On the stairs Tommy longs for Tuppence and has a fleeting dread. The scene seems 'beautifully staged'.
Julius and Jane: 'Uncle Hiram', the feud, her lost years. Her voice seems familiar to Tommy. Julius reassures her about the others.

Jane confirms Danvers gave her the papers. Her account: Holyhead, slipping away by car, the cliff path through golden gorse, the hole plugged with gorse, the begging-dog boulder, the wink on the train, the blow.
Julius promises to return and to give her 'the time of your young life'.

verbatim.text: There was a queer boulder in the path just there--for all the world like a dog sitting up begging.

voice_profile: Brisk, ironic third-person narration that stays close to Tommy, and later to Tommy and Julius, in the 'Young Adventurers' manner. The comedy comes from undercutting: Tommy's flippant, schoolboy bravado ('old bean', mock-heroic asides, 'Retire, varlet') is set against honest admissions of fear ('glad they could not hear the persistent beating of his heart'). Narrative generalisation about types ('one of those young Englishmen...') and cinema or dime-novel self-consciousness recur. Dialogue does most of the work. National idiom marks each speaker: Julius's Americanisms ('Put me wise', 'Sure thing', 'gets my goat'), the German's clipped menace, Conrad's and Number 14's cockney, Annette's broken English and French. Sir James speaks in dry, evasive legal phrasing ('Coincidences are curious things'). Chapters end on hooks: a reversal, a telegram, a twist. Double-hyphen dashes, '----' for broken-off speech and underscore emphasis are characteristic and must be retained.
